clinical_record:
A female infant was born at 35 weeks 4 days’ gestation, weighing 2152 g. She was one of monochorionic diamniotic twins; her identical twin died in utero at 24 weeks. Fetal ultrasound had shown microcephaly and ventricular enlargement. Postnatal MRI of the head revealed microcephaly, marked enlargement of both lateral ventricles without signs of elevated intracranial pressure, and severe thinning of the frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes; the temporal lobes, basal ganglia, thalamus, brain stem, and cerebellum were preserved. No intracranial hematoma or neoplastic lesions were seen. Family history was noncontributory. 

At 1 week of age, examination of the eyes showed very weak light reflexes bilaterally. The anterior chambers were slightly shallow, but there were no pupillary abnormalities, cataracts, strabismus, nystagmus, or ptosis. Funduscopic examination revealed mild optic nerve pallor with suspected peripapillary double-ring sign. The fundus had a faint reddish tone; retinal vessels appeared normal in caliber and reached the periphery. No chorioretinal dysplasia was noted.

clinical_record:
A 2-month-old full-term female with known complex congenital heart disease (single ventricle defect, double-outlet right ventricle with D-transposition of the great arteries, and an ostium secundum atrial septal defect with left superior vena cava) was admitted for evaluation of occasional cyanosis. She was in good general condition, weighed 5 kg, had an oxygen saturation of 80%, and showed no signs of respiratory distress. Her medications included furosemide and spironolactone. The team planned a pulmonary artery banding, but during the procedure the patient became hemodynamically unstable and suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest requiring cardiac massage, so the operation was aborted. To gather hemodynamic data, cardiac catheterization was performed via the left femoral artery, with the catheter tip in the single ventricle, using serial doses of nonionic iodinated contrast (Iopromide) totaling 3 mL/kg over 30 minutes. Approximately 12 hours after the procedure, the patient developed clonic movements of the left upper limb and persistent sucking motions. A noncontrast head CT obtained after this first seizure showed a slight diffuse increase in cortical density predominantly in the right frontal, parietal, and occipital lobes and, to a lesser extent, in the left parietal and occipital lobes; there was no mass effect, hemorrhage, or other intracranial abnormality.

A 64-year-old woman presented with a 2-month history of right upper abdominal pain without nausea, vomiting, chills, or fever. She had no history of hepatitis, surgery, or hereditary disease, and no underlying medical conditions. On examination, she was afebrile and oriented; there was right upper abdominal tenderness without rebound or palpable masses, no hepatosplenomegaly, and negative Murphy’s sign and shifting dullness.

Laboratory studies showed:  
• AFP 2.4 µg/l (normal 0.0–7.0)  
• CEA 11.6 µg/l (normal 0.0–5.0)  
• CA-125 32.3 KIU/l (normal 0.0–35.0)  
• CA19-9 228.0 KIU/l (normal 0.0–30.0)  
• Other liver enzymes and blood counts largely within reference ranges, except WBC 11.9×10^9/l (normal 3.5–9.5×10^9/l).

Ultrasonography revealed a heterogeneous echoic mass near the gallbladder fossa in the right liver lobe, calcifications in the right liver, multiple gallstones with gallbladder wall thickening, and enhanced pancreatic echogenicity. Contrast-enhanced CT showed a lesion in the right hepatic lobe adjacent to the gallbladder fossa, multiple enlarged hepatic hilar lymph nodes, and findings of gallstones with cholecystitis. Liver MRI demonstrated an occupying lesion in the right lobe with mild intrahepatic bile duct dilatation, raising the possibility of intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, along with gallstones and cholecystitis. No extrahepatic primary tumor was identified.

Seizures began at age 3 months, initially infrequent but progressively more frequent despite antiepileptic therapy. The parents also noted delayed motor and cognitive milestones and gradual behavioral changes, including disturbed sleep, irritability, and episodes of aimless talking. There was no family history of neurological disorders and no reported perinatal complications or trauma. 

On neurologic examination, she had significant cognitive impairment and marked left hemiparesis with brisk reflexes, consistent with an upper motor neuron pattern. Sensory examination and cranial nerves were unremarkable. Routine laboratory studies, including metabolic and infectious panels, were normal. Electroencephalography showed focal abnormal brain activity concordant with her seizure semiology. 

Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated marked asymmetry of the cerebral hemispheres, with significant atrophy of the right cerebral hemisphere and ex vacuo dilatation of the right lateral ventricle. Ipsilateral calvarial thickening and compensatory hyperpneumatization of the right sphenoid bone and bilateral mastoid air cells were evident. In the right fronto-parieto-temporal region, there were areas of cystic encephalomalacia surrounded by gliosis, suggesting a remote focal brain injury.
